messages.text: I'm 41, live alone, and just got my hours cut. Is there any help for groceries or health insurance?

I'm sorry about your hours being cut. Yes, there may be help. In Tennessee, food assistance (SNAP) and TennCare (health insurance) are two programs to check. I can look at both for you.

I have two questions to start:

1. About how much do you earn **before taxes** now, and how often are you paid (weekly, every two weeks, or monthly)?
2. Do you have any other income, like unemployment, Social Security, or child support?

Next I'll ask about rent and utilities. I'll also ask if you have a disability, since that can change the rules.
Around $260 a week before taxes, paid weekly. No other income right now.

Here's where things stand. I'm still missing a few facts to finish.

**Food assistance (SNAP):** It could be possible for you. Your pay is about $1,127 a month before taxes ($260 × 52 weeks ÷ 12). Reported Tennessee limits for one person are higher than that. But I couldn't open the official USDA or Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) pages. They blocked my access. So I can't confirm the limits or give you a dollar estimate yet. You can apply regardless. Only the agency decides.

One rule to know: adults 18 to 64 with no disability and no young children at home usually have to work, volunteer, or train about 20 hours a week to keep SNAP past 3 months. Your job may already meet that. A caseworker can confirm.

**Health insurance (TennCare):** This is harder. Tennessee did not expand Medicaid. According to [The Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/medicaid-eligibility-tennessee/), very few adults 19 to 64 without children or a disability can get TennCare. So it looks unlikely for you, but you can still apply at [tenncareconnect.tn.gov](https://tenncareconnect.tn.gov). It could change if you have a disability, are pregnant, or are a former foster youth under 26. If TennCare doesn't fit, you may be able to get lower-cost plans on the ACA Marketplace (healthcare.gov). I didn't check those rules.

To finish the food assistance check, I need two things:

1. How much is your **rent or mortgage** each month? Do you pay for **heating or cooling** separately, or other utilities, or only a phone?
2. Do you have a **disability**, or do you have children who live with you part of the time?

For free local help, you can call **211**.

Sources: [The Sycamore Institute – TennCare eligibility](https://sycamoretn.org/medicaid-eligibility-tennessee/). The SNAP limits and work-rule details come from search summaries, not official pages I could open.
Rent is $650 a month. My electric bill covers heating and AC, and I don't pay for gas or water. Just my phone, no other bills. No disability, and no kids. I live alone.

**Food assistance (SNAP) looks likely for you.** My rough estimate is about **$280 to $300 a month**. Treat that as an estimate only. Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) can decide, and you can apply.

**How I got there (monthly):**
- Your income before taxes is about $1,127 ($260 × 52 ÷ 12).
- SNAP takes off 20% of work pay, a standard deduction of $217, and a share of your housing and utility costs. Your rent is $650. You also pay an electric bill that covers heating and cooling, which SNAP counts with a set utility allowance.
- That leaves almost no countable income, so you'd get close to the one-person maximum of $306.
- The utility allowance is the shaky part. I couldn't confirm Tennessee's current amount. With a lower allowance, the estimate could drop to about $190.

**Why income looks fine:**
- Tennessee's official limit is 130% of poverty for gross income, and 100% for net income. These are from [The Sycamore Institute's SNAP page](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/). Your income looks well under both.
- Some reports say Tennessee moved to a 200% limit in June 2026, and others say it hasn't. That is unsettled. It doesn't change things for you, since you look under the lower limit.
- The 2027 amounts ($306 maximum, $217 deduction, $769 housing cap) come from search summaries. USDA's page wouldn't open for me.

**Things to know:**
- **Work rule:** You're 41 with no kids, so you'd likely need to work or train about 80 hours a month to keep SNAP beyond 3 months ([Sycamore](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)). Since your hours were cut, tell the caseworker exactly how many hours you work now.
- **Savings:** The usual limit is $3,000 in savings, not counting your home ([Sycamore](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)). That limit may not apply if the 200% rule is in place. About how much do you have in savings? You can skip this if you'd rather not say.

**Health insurance (TennCare):** This still looks **unlikely**. Tennessee didn't expand Medicaid, so most healthy adults without kids don't qualify ([Sycamore](https://sycamoretn.org/medicaid-eligibility-tennessee/)). You can still apply at [tenncareconnect.tn.gov](https://tenncareconnect.tn.gov). Also check lower-cost plans at healthcare.gov. A job-hours cut can open a special enrollment window, and you may get help paying the premium.

**Next steps:**
- Apply for SNAP through TDHS at [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices). I couldn't open that page, so I can't confirm its details.
- Call **211** for free help applying and for the current program phone numbers.
- Report your income, rent, and utilities accurately. Mistakes can lead to overpayments you'd have to pay back.

Thanks. $150 in savings is well under the usual $3,000 limit ([The Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)), so savings shouldn't get in your way. It doesn't change my estimate of about **$280 to $300 a month**. That's still only an estimate, and only TDHS decides.

**What to do now:**
1. **Apply for food assistance (SNAP)** at [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices). If you'd rather not apply online, call **211**. They can give you the local office and the current phone number.
2. **Gather proof of your income and costs.** Bring recent pay stubs that show your cut hours, your lease or a rent receipt, and an electric bill.
3. **Tell them how many hours you work now.** This matters for the work rule.
4. **Apply for TennCare** at [tenncareconnect.tn.gov](https://tenncareconnect.tn.gov). It looks unlikely for you, but applying is free. Also look at lower-cost plans at healthcare.gov.

If you apply for SNAP and it's approved, the benefit can be counted from your application date. So it's better to apply soon than to wait.

Do you want help with anything else, like food pantries or help with your electric bill? 211 can point you to both.
yeah food pantries would help, I'll call 211 about that. electric bill's ok for now, I'll ask them if it gets worse. thanks

You're welcome. Calling 211 is a good plan. They can point you to food pantries near you, and they can help with the electric bill later if you need it.

Here's a quick recap:
- **SNAP:** It looks likely, at roughly $280 to $300 a month. That's an estimate, and only TDHS decides. Apply soon at [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices).
- **TennCare:** It looks unlikely, but you can still apply at [tenncareconnect.tn.gov](https://tenncareconnect.tn.gov). Also check healthcare.gov for lower-cost plans.
- **Pantries and other help:** Call **211**.

Good luck, and come back anytime if your situation changes.

I found no official FY2027 Tennessee SNAP figures. The results show FY2026 numbers, plus a reported change to broad-based categorical eligibility that could alter the gross income test.

**Current (FY2026) limits:** Tennessee's most recent published figures, valid through September 2026, put the gross monthly income cap at $1,696 for 1 person, $2,280 for 2 people, and $3,483 for 4 people, with each additional person adding roughly $602. One source lists a slightly different 2-person figure, $2,292/month, so the two should be checked against the official table. The net income test is set at 100 percent of the Federal Poverty Level.

**Possible change:** A June 2026 report says the Tennessee Department of Human Services has adopted broad‑based categorical eligibility (BBCE), raising the SNAP gross‑income threshold from 130% to 200% of total household gross monthly income and removing asset limits for some households. An earlier January 2026 Sycamore Institute paper described this as still pending approval from the Tennessee General Assembly, so the status needs confirmation from TDHS.

**Federal context:** The federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act increases required state share of administrative costs from 50% to 75% in FFY 2027, and it requires updates to the Thrifty Food Plan to be cost-neutral.

**Not found:** I did not find FY2027 standard deduction, shelter cost, or utility allowance amounts for Tennessee. Those typically come from the USDA FNS FY2027 income eligibility standards and Tennessee DHS policy, which would be the next places to check.

Short answer: under current rules, most non-disabled adults aged 19–64 without dependent children cannot get TennCare at any income.

- **Who is excluded:** Tennessee has not expanded Medicaid, and one source says adults without dependent children can't qualify unless they are pregnant, 65 or older, blind, disabled, or a former foster youth under 26 (Adults without dependent children can't qualify unless they are pregnant, 65 or older, blind, disabled, or a former foster youth under 26.).
- **Who can qualify:** Eligible groups include parents and caretaker relatives of children under 18, pregnant women, children, people 65 or older or disabled, and former foster youth under 26 (see index 1-7 through 1-10 and 1-11 above). A separate general requirement is US citizenship or eligible immigration status, plus a Social Security number (You must live in Tennessee, be a U.S. citizen or have an eligible immigration status, and give a Social Security number.).
- **Applying:** There's no open enrollment period for Medicaid.
- **Coverage gap:** A KFF expert describes the result as no coverage for adults without dependent children, which she calls a coverage gap. Childless adults in this gap are generally left to look at ACA Marketplace options (Non-disabled adults without dependent children are generally not eligible for Medicaid regardless of income. See the ACA Marketplace coverage section below if you fall into this coverage gap.). I did not check Marketplace subsidy rules in this search.

**Caveats:** The sources disagree on the income figures. One lists parent limits at 105% of the poverty line for 2026 (Parents and caretaker relatives of children under 18 with income up to 105% of the poverty line ($2,391 a month for a family of three).), while a 2025 source lists 95%, and another guide shows 100%. Check the current income chart on the TennCare site before relying on any number. The 2026 summary also says it was checked against Division of TennCare sources on October 13, 2026.

Tennessee applies the federal ABAWD rules to adults aged 18 to under 65 who have no disability and don't live with a child under 14. The state's Department of Human Services announced these changes in September 2025 after the federal HR 1 law passed. ABAWD customers may only receive SNAP benefits for three months in a three-year period unless they work, volunteer, or participate in a job training program at least 20 hours a week (80 hours a month).

Exemptions include people under the age of 18, those 65 years of age or older, and pregnant women, among others. A January 2026 Sycamore Institute report says the federal One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB) Act changed SNAP work requirements and state-federal cost-sharing requirements.

Sources also differ on scope. One local report says the state has granted Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents (ABAWD) waivers in only seven counties that are heavily impacted by poverty and unemployment. I did not find a 2026 state notice confirming any changes to the age limit, so check the TDHS site for current details.

Search results are consistent that the FY 2027 SNAP adjustments take effect October 1, 2026, and cover the 48 states and D.C.

- **Official timing and source:** USDA published the FY 2027 adjustments on August 21, 2026, and the figures apply through September 30, 2027. USDA released the FY 2027 SNAP cost-of-living adjustments on August 21, 2026.
- **Maximum allotments (48 states and D.C.):** The one-person maximum rises to $306, the four-person maximum to $1,023, and the eight-person maximum to $1,841. Each additional person (9–17) adds $225, and 18 or more people is $3,887.
- **Standard deduction:** It is $217 for households of one to three, $229 for four, $268 for five, and $308 for six or more. The standard deduction varies by household size, and fiscal year 2027 values are $217 for one to three members and $229, $268, and $308 for four, five, and six or more members.
- **Excess shelter cap:** It rises to $769, up from $744 in FY 2026. The homeless shelter deduction rises to $205.66. Maximum excess shelter deduction was $744 in FY 2026 and is $769 in FY 2027.

**Tennessee SNAP Eligibility Limits and Rules**

- **Gross income limit:** Monthly gross income cannot exceed 130% of the poverty level, or $3,483 for a family of four. The article does not mention a 200% limit.
- **Net income limit:** Monthly net income cannot exceed 100% of the poverty level, or $2,680 for a family of four.
- **Earned income deduction:** A 20% deduction applies to earned income when calculating net income.
- **Standard utility allowance:** The article does not give this amount.
- **Asset limit:** Most households are limited to $3,000 in countable assets. Households with a person who has a disability or is age 60 or older are limited to $4,500. The home and retirement plans are excluded.
- **Work requirements:** There are two:
  - **General work requirement:** Able-bodied adults ages 16 to 59 must register for work or join an employment or training program. They cannot quit a job without another lined up, cut hours without reasonable cause, or refuse suitable job offers.
  - **ABAWD work requirement:** Able-bodied adults ages 18 to 64 without a dependent under 14 must work or report at least 80 hours per month to receive more than three months of benefits in a three-year period. Before the federal OBBB Act, this applied to ages 18 to 54 without a dependent under 18. The Act also removed exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and people ages 24 and older who aged out of foster care.

The article also notes that TDHS is pursuing state rule changes, pending legislative approval, that would align SNAP income limits with TANF.
